knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)

**Base treatment (fixed across all interaction models in this series):**
`W = 1(type == 1)` vs. `type == 0`, restricted to
`name_ethnicity %in% c("Canada", "Chinese", "Indian", "Pakistani")`. Type 0 to
Type 1 changes *only* the applicant's name --- education and work-experience
origin are held at "Canadian" for both --- so `W` isolates the pure name
effect, uncontaminated by the foreign-credential confounds present in Types
2--4. This is narrower than the Type 0--4 comparison used in the Table 4/5
baseline replication, and matches TC's instruction to restrict the causal
forest step to this cleaner contrast.

**This model's moderator:** `female`, i.e. whether the resume carries a female
name. We interact `female` with key education and experience signals
(`ba_quality`, `exp_highquality`, `same_exp`, `ma`, `extracurricular_skills`,
`language_skills`, `reference`, `accreditation`) to test whether returns to
these resume characteristics differ by gender.

This directly operationalizes mechanisms documented in the audit and
discrimination literature:

- **Gender × education quality (`female × ba_quality`)**  
  Quadlin (2018, *ASR*) shows that high academic achievement pays off more for
  men than for women, especially in male-typed fields; high-achieving women are
  sometimes penalized on likability/fit dimensions despite strong credentials
  [62][64][66]. This motivates expecting asymmetric returns to top-200 university
  degrees by gender.

- **Gender × experience quality (`female × exp_highquality`)**  
  Audit and field-experiment evidence indicates that the value of experience is
  gendered: in some contexts, men's experience is weighted more heavily, and
  employers may use different criteria (competence vs. likability) when
  evaluating equally experienced men and women [62][64][68]. Occupational
  segregation further implies that the same “high-quality” experience may be
  interpreted differently depending on gender [66][67][69].

- **Gender × multinational / same-exp (`female × same_exp`)**  
  Multinational-firm experience is a prestige signal that may interact with
  gendered expectations about mobility, commitment, and fit. Meta-analytic and
  audit evidence shows that gender bias is stronger in male-dominated contexts,
  suggesting that cosmopolitan signals may not benefit women symmetrically
  [66][67][69].

- **Gender × Master's degree (`female × ma`)**  
  Quadlin (2018) and related work imply that advanced degrees can signal
  differently by gender: strong credentials can backfire for women if they
  violate gendered expectations, especially in male-typed occupations
  [62][64][66].

- **Gender × extracurriculars, language, references, accreditation**  
  These are additional productivity/fit signals. Gender-composition and
  occupational-segregation findings suggest that any signal’s return can be
  moderated by gender because employers evaluate “fit” through gendered lenses,
  particularly in male- vs. female-dominated jobs [66][67][69][70].

**On standard errors and clustering.**  
The original Oreopoulos (2011) Stata code uses robust SEs only, never clustering.
Our design sends multiple resumes to the same employer (typically ~4 per firm),
so observations within `firmid` are not independent. We therefore:

- Report **robust SEs** (HC1) to match the original approach.
- Report **clustered SEs by `firmid`** (CR2) as our preferred specification,
  following our group proposal and standard practice for audit studies with
  within-firm randomization.

Both are reported side by side so the deviation is explicit and auditable.

# Setup

```{r setup}
required_packages <- c("haven", "estimatr", "dplyr", "modelsummary")
missing_packages  <- setdiff(required_packages, rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(missing_packages) > 0) {
  install.packages(missing_packages, repos = "[https://cloud.r-project.org](https://cloud.r-project.org)")
}
library(haven)
library(estimatr)
library(dplyr)
library(modelsummary)

data_path <- file.path("data", "oreopoulos-resume-study-replication-data-file.dta")
if (!file.exists(data_path)) {
  stop("Data file not found. Expected it at: ", normalizePath(data_path, mustWork = FALSE))
}
df <- read_dta(data_path)
```

# Sample construction

```{r sample}
df_int2 <- df %>%
  filter(
    type %in% c(0, 1),
    name_ethnicity %in% c("Canada", "Chinese", "Indian", "Pakistani")
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    W              = as.numeric(type == 1),   # 1 = foreign name (Type 1), 0 = Type 0 baseline
    fall_data      = factor(fall_data),
    # Recode moderators and controls; treat NA as 0 where structurally undefined
    female                 = ifelse(is.na(female), 0, female),
    ba_quality             = ifelse(is.na(ba_quality), 0, ba_quality),
    extracurricular_skills = ifelse(is.na(extracurricular_skills), 0, extracurricular_skills),
    ma                     = ifelse(is.na(ma), 0, ma),
    same_exp               = ifelse(is.na(same_exp), 0, same_exp),
    exp_highquality        = ifelse(is.na(exp_highquality), 0, exp_highquality),
    language_skills        = ifelse(is.na(language_skills), 0, language_skills),
    accreditation          = ifelse(is.na(accreditation), 0, accreditation),
    reference              = ifelse(is.na(reference), 0, reference)
  )

cat("Analysis sample size:", nrow(df_int2), "\n")
cat("Treatment (W) distribution:\n")
print(table(df_int2$W))
cat("Gender distribution:\n")
print(table(df_int2$female))
```

# Model A: `callback ~ female × type + all other controls (main effects only)`

We first estimate a parsimonious interaction model focusing on whether the effect of having a foreign name (Type 1 vs. Type 0) differs by gender, while still controlling for all other resume characteristics as main effects.

```{r fit-mA}
# (1) Robust SEs only
mA_robust <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ female * W +
    ba_quality + exp_highquality + same_exp + ma +
    extracurricular_skills + language_skills + reference + accreditation +
    fall_data,
  data = df_int2, se_type = "HC1"
)

# (2) Clustered by firmid
mA_clustered <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ female * W +
    ba_quality + exp_highquality + same_exp + ma +
    extracurricular_skills + language_skills + reference + accreditation +
    fall_data,
  data = df_int2, clusters = firmid, se_type = "CR2"
)
```

## Table: Model A (female × type)

```{r table-mA, results = "asis"}
modelsummary(
  list(
    "Robust SE (Oreopoulos-style)" = mA_robust,
    "Clustered by firm (proposal)"  = mA_clustered
  ),
  stars    = TRUE,
  coef_omit = "fall_data",
  gof_omit  = "IC|Log|Adj|F|RMSE",
  title     = "Model A: Gender × Type (Foreign Name) Interaction"
)
```

**Coefficient of interest:** `female:W`  
- A **negative and significant** estimate implies that the foreign-name penalty (Type 1 vs. Type 0) is larger for women than for men, consistent with intersectional or compounded disadvantages for foreign-named women (Oreopoulos, 2011; Quillian et al., 2017).  
- A **positive and significant** estimate would imply that the foreign-name penalty is smaller for women (or that foreign-named women are relatively favored compared to foreign-named men).  
- A **null** estimate would suggest that the name effect is similar across genders.

All other resume signals (`ba_quality`, `exp_highquality`, `same_exp`, `ma`, etc.) are included as **controls only** (no interactions) in this model.

---

# Model B: `callback ~ female × (education/experience signals) + type + controls`

We now estimate the richer specification that allows the return to education and experience signals to vary by gender. Here, `type` (i.e., `W`) is included as a main effect only.

```{r fit-mB}
# (1) Robust SEs only
mB_robust <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ 
    female * (
      ba_quality +
      exp_highquality +
      same_exp +
      ma +
      extracurricular_skills +
      language_skills +
      reference +
      accreditation
    ) +
    W + fall_data,
  data = df_int2, se_type = "HC1"
)

# (2) Clustered by firmid
mB_clustered <- lm_robust(
  callback ~ 
    female * (
      ba_quality +
      exp_highquality +
      same_exp +
      ma +
      extracurricular_skills +
      language_skills +
      reference +
      accreditation
    ) +
    W + fall_data,
  data = df_int2, clusters = firmid, se_type = "CR2"
)
```

## Table: Model B (female × education/experience signals)

```{r table-mB, results = "asis"}
modelsummary(
  list(
    "Robust SE (Oreopoulos-style)" = mB_robust,
    "Clustered by firm (proposal)"  = mB_clustered
  ),
  stars    = TRUE,
  coef_omit = "fall_data",
  gof_omit  = "IC|Log|Adj|F|RMSE",
  title     = "Model B: Gender × Education/Experience Signals"
)
```

## Interpretation guide for Model B

Focus on the interaction terms:

- **`female:ba_quality`**  
  Tests whether the return to a top-200 university degree differs by gender.  
  Quadlin (2018) and related audit work suggest high-achieving women may not
  benefit as much as men from elite credentials, especially in male-typed
  contexts [62][64][66].

- **`female:exp_highquality`**  
  Tests whether high-quality work experience yields symmetric returns by gender.  
  Evidence on gendered evaluation of experience and occupational segregation
  implies possible asymmetries [62][66][68][69].

- **`female:same_exp`**  
  Tests whether multinational-firm experience (same_exp) benefits women as much
  as men. Given gendered fit perceptions and occupational sorting, we allow for
  heterogeneous returns [66][67][69].

- **`female:ma`**  
  Tests whether a Canadian Master’s degree has different returns by gender.  
  Quadlin (2018) shows advanced credentials can backfire for women if they
  violate gendered expectations, supporting the hypothesis of asymmetric returns
  [62][64][66].

- **`female:extracurricular_skills`, `female:language_skills`,
  `female:reference`, `female:accreditation`**  
  These capture whether additional productivity/fit signals (activities,
  language fluency, Canadian references, foreign-education accreditation) are
  valued differently for women. Gender-composition and audit evidence suggest
  that any such signal can be evaluated through gendered lenses, especially in
  male- vs. female-dominated jobs [66][67][69][70].

A **negative and significant** interaction coefficient means that the
corresponding signal increases the callback probability *less* for women than
for men (or possibly decreases it), consistent with gendered standards for
competence, likability, and fit documented in the audit literature
[62][64][66][67][69][70].
